messages.subject: Improved Mapping Methods
parts:
Hi all,

Here are some thoughts on QTL mapping and the evolution of its methods. My experience is with plant populations.

Standard regression approaches run into trouble with increasing marker density. Over fitting appears to be a common problem, even with methods like inclusive composite interval mapping, and particularly when trying to decide if one QTL peak is really two.

Modeling QTL as random effects can result in over-shrinking effects.

Use of the kinship (either leave one chromosome out or spectral decomposition with removal of markers linked to the one being tested) appears to be really helpful in this matter.

What I'm wondering, however, is the best way to decide which flanking markers in LD with the one being tested, if any, should be used as cofactors. Is this aspect of mapping still an art or arbitrary based on the model choices?
